title: How to Know What Is True
question: When a study, a dashboard or a trusted colleague says something works, how do you decide how much to believe it and what to do about it?

overview.text: Executives are paid to act on evidence they did not produce: analyses from their staff, studies from consultants and vendors, research from universities, and the apparent lessons of their own experience. Most of that evidence is neither worthless nor conclusive. This week builds the skills to tell the difference and to act sensibly in between.

The week moves in five steps. Lesson 1 separates signal from noise: regression to the mean, confidence intervals, p-values and power, and the Bayesian logic that connects them to Week 1’s base rates. Lesson 2 examines the replication crisis as a system — flexible analysis, low power and selective publication — that operates inside organizations as well as in journals. Lesson 3 is a compact course in causal inference for executives: counterfactuals, confounding and selection, randomized trials, and the quasi-experimental designs that have transformed economics and policy evaluation. Lesson 4 adds the questions that remain after a design is credible: effect size, measurement, Goodhart’s law, external validity and survivorship. Lesson 5 asks how to combine imperfect evidence, using evidence hierarchies and meta-analysis without being ruled by them.

The Evidence Lab lets you generate thousands of simulated studies and watch exaggerated effects, false positives and missed effects emerge from design choices. The case, set in a health system, puts two respected executives on opposite sides of the same data. The assignment asks you to critique a real published study with a structured rubric. The aim is not cynicism. It is calibrated belief: knowing how much a piece of evidence should move you, and how to design your organization’s decisions so that it learns.

objectives: Distinguish signal from noise using regression to the mean, confidence intervals, p-values and statistical power.
Explain how researcher degrees of freedom, low power and publication bias produce exaggerated and false findings, and evaluate remedies.
Identify confounding, selection and collider bias and match randomized and quasi-experimental designs to causal questions.
Critique a study’s effect size, measurement, external validity and susceptibility to metric gaming.
Combine several imperfect lines of evidence into a stated degree of belief and a proportionate decision.

lessons.title: Signal, Noise and the Meaning of p
lessons.summary: Every measurement mixes signal with noise; regression to the mean, confidence intervals, p-values and power are tools for keeping the two apart.
objectives: Explain regression to the mean and identify it in a performance story that offers a causal explanation instead.
Interpret a confidence interval and a p-value correctly and state what each does not tell you.
Use statistical power and prior plausibility to judge how much a significant result should change your belief.
lessons.executive: Most numbers that reach your desk are a true level plus luck. When you select people, units or quarters because they were extreme, the luck you selected on will not repeat, so they drift back toward average whatever you do: regression to the mean. A p-value tells you how surprising the data would be if nothing were going on; it does not tell you the probability the claim is true, how big the effect is, or whether it matters. Ask for the estimate with its confidence interval, the sample size, and how plausible the claim was before the data. Treat a small study’s significant result as a hypothesis, not a finding.

explore.text: A regional hospital system ranks its twenty emergency departments every quarter on door-to-provider time. The three worst departments are placed on an improvement plan: a consultant visits, managers attend a workshop, and dashboards are posted in the break rooms. Next quarter, all three improve markedly. The three best departments, which received a congratulatory letter, all get worse. The chief operating officer concludes that improvement plans work and that praise breeds complacency. This scenario is hypothetical, but the pattern is everywhere.

Before reading on: what would you expect to happen to the three worst departments next quarter if the improvement plan had done nothing at all? Write down a number of departments (0–3) you would expect to improve, and why.

Tversky and Kahneman described the same pattern in flight training. Instructors noticed that cadets who were praised after an unusually smooth landing usually did worse on the next attempt, while cadets criticized after a rough landing usually improved. The instructors concluded that criticism works and praise backfires. The authors’ point was that the instructors had discovered regression to the mean and mistaken it for a causal effect of their feedback ([Tversky & Kahneman, 1974](R-tversky-1974-judgment)).

This lesson is about the difference between signal and noise. It covers four tools that every executive who reads evidence must handle comfortably: regression to the mean, the confidence interval, the p-value and statistical power. None of them requires advanced mathematics. All of them are misunderstood by many of the people who will present evidence to you.

understand.text: Observed performance is a true level plus luck

Think of any measured result — a department’s quarterly wait time, a fund’s annual return, a salesperson’s monthly bookings, a hitter’s batting average over three weeks — as the sum of two parts: a stable underlying level and a transient component that does not repeat. The transient part includes genuine randomness, measurement error, and temporary circumstances such as a flu outbreak or an easy schedule. The proportion of variation that is stable is called the *reliability* of the measure. When reliability is high, last period predicts next period well. When it is low, last period is mostly noise.

Now select units because they were extreme. The worst three departments are, on average, departments with a somewhat worse true level *and* a bad draw of luck in that quarter. Next quarter the true level persists but the luck is redrawn, so on average they move back toward the middle. The same is true in reverse for the best performers. Regression to the mean is not a force and it does not require any intervention. It is a consequence of selecting on a noisy measure. The lower the reliability and the more extreme the selection, the larger the expected regression.

understand.text: A simple prediction rule follows. Your best forecast of next period is not last period’s observed value but a weighted average of it and the group mean, with the weight on the observed value equal to the measure’s reliability. If a quarterly metric has a reliability of 0.4, a department that was 10 minutes worse than average should be expected to be about 4 minutes worse next quarter. If the improvement plan produces a 6-minute gain, most of it was expected anyway. The only clean way to know whether the plan did anything is to compare treated departments with similarly extreme departments that were not treated, ideally chosen at random.

understand.title: Prerequisite: samples, sampling variability and the standard error

blocks.text: A *sample* is the subset of cases you actually observe; the *population* is the larger set you want to learn about. If you surveyed a different random sample, you would get a different average. That variation from sample to sample is *sampling variability*. Its typical size is the *standard error*: roughly the standard deviation of individual cases divided by the square root of the sample size. Quadrupling a sample halves the standard error. This square-root law is why small samples bounce around so much and why doubling a pilot’s size buys less precision than intuition suggests.

Two numbers therefore always travel together: the estimate (for example, a 3-point improvement) and its uncertainty (for example, a standard error of 2 points). An estimate without its uncertainty is half a fact.

understand.text: Confidence intervals

A 95% confidence interval is a range constructed by a procedure that, across many repeated samples, would capture the true value 95% of the time. In practice, read it as the range of effect sizes reasonably compatible with the data under the analysis assumptions. Two features matter more than whether it excludes zero. Its *location* tells you the most plausible magnitudes. Its *width* tells you how much the study actually taught you. An interval from −1 to +9 minutes and an interval from +3.8 to +4.2 minutes can both have the same center; only the second one supports a confident operational decision.
What a p-value is, and is not

A p-value is the probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as what was observed, *if* a specified statistical model — usually one in which the true effect is zero — were correct, and if all its assumptions held. In 2016 the American Statistical Association issued its first formal statement on a matter of statistical practice to correct widespread misuse. Among its principles: p-values can indicate how incompatible data are with a specified model; they do not measure the probability that the hypothesis is true or that the data arose by chance alone; decisions should not rest only on whether a p-value crosses a threshold; proper inference requires full reporting; and a p-value does not measure the size or importance of an effect ([Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016](R-wasserstein-2016-asa)).

understand.text: Power: the probability of detecting what is really there

*Statistical power* is the probability that a study will produce a significant result when a true effect of a given size exists. It depends on the size of the effect, the noise in the measure, the sample size and the significance threshold. A study of 20 people per group looking for a modest effect (about a third of a standard deviation) has power of roughly 15%: it will miss the true effect about 85% of the time. Low power has a less obvious cost, taken up in [Lesson 2](#w04-l2): when a low-powered study does reach significance, its estimate is usually far too large.

understand.title: Methodological note: why the p-value is not the probability you want

blocks.text: The question an executive cares about is: given this result, how likely is it that the effect is real? That is a *posterior* probability. Bayes’ rule says it depends on three things: the prior probability that the tested idea is true, the power of the study, and the significance threshold. Suppose your analytics team tests 100 product ideas, of which perhaps 10 genuinely work. With power of 50% and a 5% threshold, about 5 of the 10 real effects come back significant, and about 4.5 of the 90 null ideas come back significant by chance. Roughly half of the “wins” are false. Raise power to 80% and only 8 of about 12.5 wins are real; lower the prior to 1 in 100 and false wins dominate.

This is the logic of Ioannidis’s argument that, under realistic priors, power and bias, many claimed findings in some fields are likely to be false ([Ioannidis, 2005](R-ioannidis-2005-most)). It also explains why the same p-value should move you more for a plausible, mechanistically grounded claim than for a surprising one. Week 1’s base-rate reasoning is the same arithmetic applied to research.

challenge.text: Three objections deserve a serious answer. First, some argue that p-values are fine and the problem is misinterpretation, so better training rather than new methods is the remedy. That is partly right: a p-value correctly understood is a legitimate measure of surprise under a model. But a tool that is routinely misread by trained researchers is a poor tool for executive communication. Estimates with intervals carry the same information and more.

Second, Bayesian analysts argue that executives should ask for posterior probabilities directly. That is attractive, but priors can be chosen to flatter a conclusion, and a Bayesian analysis with a hidden prior is no more transparent than a frequentist one with a hidden analysis plan. The disciplined position is to ask for the prior to be stated and for the result to be shown under a skeptical prior as well.

Third, not everything that drifts toward the mean is regression. Interventions can work, and true levels can change. The ASA statement’s emphasis on context and on full reporting is a reminder that statistical tools never substitute for design: the question is always what the comparison group was ([Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016](R-wasserstein-2016-asa)).

challenge.title: Executive twist: the board wants a yes or no

blocks.text: You chair a review of a pilot in a financial-services contact center. The pilot reduced complaint rates by an estimated 11%, with a 95% interval from −2% to +23%. The p-value is 0.09. The vendor calls it “directionally positive”; your finance lead calls it “not significant, so it failed”. Both are reasoning from the threshold. The interval says the program could plausibly do nothing or could do a great deal. The decision turns on costs: if extending the pilot is cheap and reversible, buying more information is worth it; if full rollout is expensive and hard to undo, it is not yet justified. Your job is to reframe the decision around the range of plausible effects and the cost of being wrong in each direction, not around p.

apply.text: Player development is an ideal environment for regression to the mean, because nearly every early-season statistic has low reliability and nearly every intervention is triggered by an extreme. A hitter who opens the season badly is given a mechanical adjustment and a new routine; three weeks later he has improved and the adjustment gets the credit. A pitcher with an exceptional first month is promoted and then “struggles to adjust to the level”. Some of each story may be true. The disciplined question is how much improvement or decline you would have predicted with no intervention, given the reliability of the measure over that sample.

items: Before an intervention, record the forecast for the player without it (the observed value shrunk toward his own longer-run baseline or the group mean).
Judge the intervention by performance relative to that forecast, not relative to the slump.
Where possible, compare with similarly extreme players who did not receive the intervention, or randomize which players receive it first.
Prefer process measures with higher reliability over short-sample outcomes when you need to judge quickly.

apply.text: The same discipline applies in other domains. A government agency that audits the schools with the worst test scores will see improvement next year; a private-equity firm that replaces the managers of its worst-performing portfolio companies will see recoveries; an asset manager that hires last year’s top fund will often be disappointed. In each case the honest benchmark is the regression-adjusted forecast, not last year’s extreme.

Worked problem: a quarterly employee-engagement score has a reliability of 0.5 across teams. A team scores 20 points below the company average and receives coaching. Next quarter it is 6 points below average. How much of the 14-point improvement would you have expected without coaching? (Answer: about 10 points, because the expected position is 0.5 × −20 = −10. The coaching is credited with at most about 4 points, and even that needs a comparison group.)

retain.text: Observed results combine a stable level with transient noise. Selecting on extremes guarantees drift back toward the mean, which looks like an effect of whatever you did in between. A p-value measures surprise under a null model, not the truth of a claim or the size of an effect; confidence intervals and power tell you how much a study can teach you. How much a significant result should move you depends on prior plausibility and power.
Explain to a colleague, in two sentences, why the worst performers on a noisy metric usually improve.
List three things a p-value does not tell you.
Why does the same p-value deserve less belief when power is low and the hypothesis is surprising?

takeaways: Selecting on extremes of a noisy measure produces regression to the mean with or without any intervention.
Judge an intervention against a regression-adjusted forecast or a comparison group, never against the slump that triggered it.
A p-value is the probability of data this extreme under a null model — not the probability the claim is true, and not a measure of importance.
Ask for estimates with confidence intervals, sample sizes and power; the interval’s width shows how much was learned.
The credibility of a significant result depends on prior plausibility and power, as Bayes’ rule makes explicit.

check.prompt: A sales organization gives its bottom-decile reps an intensive coaching program. Their bookings rise substantially the next quarter. What is the most important missing piece of information?

options.text: The satisfaction scores the reps gave the coaching program.
How much similarly ranked reps who were not coached improved over the same period.
Whether the improvement was statistically significant.
Whether top-decile reps declined over the same period.

check.explanation: Bottom-decile reps were selected partly for bad luck, so they would be expected to improve without coaching. Only a comparison with similarly extreme reps who were not coached separates the coaching effect from regression to the mean. Significance of the before-after change would not help, because the regression itself is a real, systematic change.

optionFeedback.a: Satisfaction with a program is not evidence of its effect on bookings.
optionFeedback.c: A before-after change can be highly significant and still be entirely regression to the mean.
optionFeedback.d: Decline at the top is what regression predicts too; it does not isolate the coaching effect.

lessons.title: The Replication Crisis and the Garden of Forking Paths
lessons.summary: Low power, flexible analysis and selective publication combine to fill literatures with exaggerated and false findings; preregistration and registered reports are partial remedies.
objectives: Explain how researcher degrees of freedom and publication bias inflate false positives and effect sizes.
Interpret type-S and type-M errors and estimate when a significant result is likely to be exaggerated.
Evaluate preregistration and registered reports as remedies, including their limits.
lessons.executive: A large share of published behavioral science has not replicated, and the published effects that do replicate are usually smaller than first reported. The cause is not mainly fraud. It is a system: small studies, many defensible analytic choices made after seeing data, and journals and managers who reward significant, surprising results. The same system operates inside organizations whenever analysts can choose metrics, segments and stopping points after the fact. Ask whether the analysis was specified before the data arrived, how many outcomes were examined, and how large the sample was. Expect real effects to be smaller than the first study suggested.

explore.text: Imagine a technology company’s growth team that reports a string of successful experiments: a new checkout button lifted conversion 9%, a revised onboarding email lifted retention 12%, a loyalty badge lifted engagement 15%. Finance notices that the company’s overall conversion, retention and engagement have barely moved in two years. Every experiment was “significant”. Where did the gains go? This scenario is hypothetical, but its arithmetic is exactly the arithmetic of the replication crisis.
Before reading on: list three ways an honest analyst on that team could produce a significant result even if none of the changes worked.

In 2015 a collaboration of researchers repeated 100 studies published in three leading psychology journals. About 97% of the originals had reported significant results; about 36% of the replications did, and the average replication effect was roughly half the original ([Open Science Collaboration, 2015](R-osc-2015-estimating)). Large-scale replication projects in other fields have produced similar warnings. The question for an executive is not whether psychology is broken but which mechanisms produce this pattern — because the same mechanisms operate in your own organization’s analytics.

understand.text: Mechanism 1: researcher degrees of freedom

Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn showed that common analytic decisions, each defensible on its own, can push the false-positive rate far above the nominal 5%. Their list included choosing among several dependent variables, deciding whether to collect more data after checking significance, adding or dropping covariates, and dropping experimental conditions. Combined in a simulation, such flexibility produced false-positive rates above 60%. In a deliberately absurd demonstration, they “showed” that listening to a particular song made participants younger ([Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn, 2011](R-simmons-2011-false-positive)).

The deeper point, often called the *garden of forking paths*, is that the analyst need not try many analyses consciously. If the choice of analysis depends on the data — which outcome looks cleanest, which outliers seem odd, which subgroup is interesting — the effective number of comparisons is large even when only one is run. A p-value is valid only for an analysis that would have been run regardless of the data.
Mechanism 2: low power and the significance filter

Gelman and Carlin argued that the main danger of underpowered studies is not missed effects but misleading discoveries. When power is low, only estimates that happen to be much larger than the truth can clear the significance threshold. Conditional on being significant, such estimates are systematically exaggerated — a *type M* (magnitude) error — and with very low power a non-trivial share have the wrong sign — a *type S* (sign) error ([Gelman & Carlin, 2014](R-gelman-2014-beyond)).

understand.text: Mechanism 3: publication bias

If significant results are published, promoted or presented and non-significant ones are filed away, the visible literature is a filtered sample. Even if every study were analyzed honestly, the filter alone exaggerates average effects and can manufacture an apparent effect from nothing. Inside organizations the file drawer is the pilot that “didn’t pan out” and was never written up.

A useful benchmark comes from Registered Reports, a format in which a journal reviews and accepts the study design before the results exist. Scheel, Schijen and Lakens compared standard psychology papers with Registered Reports: about 96% of standard papers supported their first hypothesis, against about 44% of Registered Reports ([Scheel, Schijen & Lakens, 2021](R-scheel-2021-excess)). The comparison is not randomized — Registered Reports may test riskier ideas — but a gap of that size is hard to explain without selective reporting.

understand.title: Prerequisite: false positives, false negatives and the 5% convention

blocks.text: A *false positive* (type I error) is concluding there is an effect when there is none. A *false negative* (type II error) is missing an effect that exists. The conventional significance threshold of 5% caps the false-positive rate *for one pre-specified test when the null is true*. It says nothing about what happens when you run twenty tests and report the best, when you stop collecting data the moment p dips below .05, or when only significant results are shown to you. Each of those practices quietly raises the real false-positive rate. If you test ten independent outcomes on a program with no effect at all and report any that is significant, you will “find” something about 40% of the time.

understand.title: Methodological note: why significant-and-small-sample is a warning sign, not a strength

blocks.text: People often reason that a result significant in a small sample must reflect a large effect, since it overcame so much noise. Gelman and Carlin’s analysis shows the opposite inference is safer. In a small sample, the standard error is large, so the threshold for significance is a large estimate. If prior knowledge suggests the true effect is modest, then significance in a small sample implies the estimate is mostly noise in a favorable direction. The *exaggeration ratio* — expected significant estimate divided by true effect — can exceed two or three when power is below 20%. The remedy is a *design analysis*: before believing an estimate, ask what effect size is plausible from external evidence, compute the power the study had for that effect, and from that infer the likely exaggeration.

Gelman and Carlin recommend that the plausible effect come from outside the study, such as prior literature or domain knowledge, rather than from the study’s own estimate, which is precisely the number in doubt ([Gelman & Carlin, 2014](R-gelman-2014-beyond)).

challenge.text: The size of the problem is debated. Gilbert, King, Pettigrew and Wilson argued that the Open Science Collaboration’s design could not support its pessimistic conclusion: single replications have limited power, some replications differed from the original populations or procedures, and with these factors accounted for the results looked less alarming ([Gilbert et al., 2016](R-gilbert-2016-comment)). The original authors replied that the critique misread their design, and most methodologists accept that replication rates in that literature were low even if the exact number is uncertain ([Open Science Collaboration, 2015](R-osc-2015-estimating)). Two lessons survive the debate: a single failed replication is itself weak evidence, and interpreting replications requires the same attention to power and fidelity as interpreting originals.

Another objection is that the logic is too pessimistic. Ioannidis’s model shows that the share of true findings depends heavily on assumed priors, power and bias; in fields with strong theory, large samples and pre-specified analyses, most findings can be true ([Ioannidis, 2005](R-ioannidis-2005-most)). The replication crisis is not evidence that research is useless. It is evidence that the reliability of a literature can be predicted from its design features.

Remedies have limits too. Preregistration constrains forking paths only if the plan is specific and deviations are reported; vague plans and undisclosed deviations are common. Registered Reports address publication bias but not poor measurement or weak theory. Large replications can estimate an average effect precisely while missing that it varies across contexts. And some exploratory flexibility is valuable: the aim is not to forbid exploration but to label it honestly and confirm it on fresh data.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the analyst who is always right

blocks.text: A gifted analyst on your staff has produced eleven “wins” in a row from internal pilots. Colleagues admire the record; you are uneasy. You cannot see the analysis decisions, the pilots that were dropped, or what was planned in advance. Accusing the analyst would be unfair and damaging. Changing the system is not: require short pre-analysis plans for decisions above a threshold, keep a register of every pilot started, and ask for a hold-out confirmation before scaling. Frame it as protection for the analyst’s credibility, which it is.

apply.text: For an executive, the replication crisis translates into a short set of questions you can ask of any result, internal or external. They do not require you to re-run the analysis.

apply.text: In professional baseball, the forking-paths problem is acute because the data are rich. An analyst evaluating a new hitting drill can choose among exit velocity, launch angle, hard-hit rate, whiff rate and a dozen derived metrics; among different windows; among levels and handedness splits. With enough choices, something will move. A department that wants to learn rather than to celebrate can pre-commit to a primary outcome and window, report every metric examined, and treat secondary findings as hypotheses for the next cohort. Staggered rollouts across affiliates, with the order chosen at random, turn routine program launches into replications.

The same structure appears elsewhere. Pharmaceutical regulators require trial registration and pre-specified primary endpoints for exactly these reasons. Financial firms back-testing trading strategies face the same problem as “data snooping” and reserve untouched out-of-sample periods. Product teams that run many A/B tests and stop when significance appears inflate false positives in the same way as a lab that peeks at its data. The remedy in every field is the same family: pre-commitment, full reporting, adequate samples and confirmation.

Worked problem: your team ran 20 independent A/B tests of minor interface changes, none of which (unknown to you) had any effect. How many “significant” results at p < .05 should you expect? (About one. If the team presents one win and does not mention the other nineteen tests, the win is almost certainly noise.)

retain.text: Exaggerated and false findings arise systematically from three interacting mechanisms: flexible analysis decided after seeing the data, low power combined with a significance filter, and selective publication. Significant results from small studies are usually overestimates. Pre-commitment and full reporting reduce the problem; they do not replace good measurement or theory.

takeaways: Most failed findings come from a system of incentives and flexibility, not from fraud.
Undisclosed analytic flexibility can raise the real false-positive rate far above 5%.
In low-powered studies, significant estimates are exaggerated (type M) and sometimes have the wrong sign (type S).
Publication filters manufacture inflated literatures; Registered Reports show far fewer positive results.
Ask for pre-specified outcomes, all analyses examined, power, and confirmation on fresh data.

check.prompt: Which interpretation of this report is most defensible?

stimulus.text: Fictional abstract: A consulting firm trained 24 managers in a new feedback method and compared them with 24 untrained managers. Of 9 engagement measures collected, “team voice” improved significantly (d = 0.85, p = .01). The authors conclude the method produces large improvements in team voice.

options.text: The large effect is especially convincing because it was detected in a small sample.
The finding is a reasonable hypothesis, but the estimate is probably inflated and may be a false positive given nine outcomes and a small sample.
The result should be dismissed because p-values are invalid.
The result is confirmed because d = 0.85 is a large effect by conventional standards.

check.explanation: Nine outcomes with one significant result is close to what chance alone produces, and a small sample means only large estimates can reach significance, so the effect size is likely exaggerated. The right status is an unconfirmed hypothesis to test with a pre-specified outcome in a larger sample.

optionFeedback.a: This is the reverse of the correct inference: small samples make significant estimates more likely to be exaggerated.
optionFeedback.c: p-values are valid for what they measure; the problem here is multiple outcomes and low power.
optionFeedback.d: The conventional label says nothing about whether the estimate is reliable.

check.prompt: What is the main problem that a Registered Report addresses that ordinary preregistration alone does not?

options.text: Measurement error in the outcome.
Publication decisions that depend on whether the results were significant.
Lack of random assignment.
Low external validity.

check.explanation: In a Registered Report the journal commits to publish based on the question and design before results exist, so the result cannot determine publication. Preregistration alone constrains analytic flexibility but does not stop a null study from staying in the file drawer.

optionFeedback.a: Neither format fixes a poor measure.
optionFeedback.c: Registered Reports can be observational; they do not impose randomization.
optionFeedback.d: Generalizability depends on the sample and setting, not on the publication format.

lessons.title: Causal Inference for Executives
lessons.summary: Every causal claim is a comparison with a counterfactual; randomization and a handful of quasi-experimental designs make that comparison credible, each under one checkable assumption.
objectives: Define a causal effect as a counterfactual comparison and identify confounding, selection and collider bias in a causal story.
Explain the logic and key assumption of randomized trials, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity and instrumental variables.
Choose an appropriate design for an organizational question given practical constraints.
lessons.executive: A causal claim compares what happened with what would have happened otherwise. You never observe both, so every causal estimate depends on a comparison group standing in for the counterfactual. Correlations mislead when something else drives both variables (confounding), when the people who receive a program differ from those who do not (selection), or when you analyze only cases filtered on an outcome (collider bias). Randomization solves these problems by design. When you cannot randomize, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity and instrumental variables can work, each resting on one assumption you should ask the analyst to defend in plain language.

explore.text: For decades, observational studies found that women who took hormone therapy after menopause had lower rates of heart disease, and many physicians prescribed it partly for that reason. When the Women’s Health Initiative randomized healthy postmenopausal women to combined hormone therapy or placebo, the trial was stopped early: overall risks, including coronary heart disease and breast cancer, exceeded benefits ([Rossouw et al., 2002](R-rossouw-2002-risks)). A leading explanation for the earlier association is that women who chose hormone therapy tended to be healthier and wealthier in ways that also protected their hearts.
Before reading on: name two variables that could make hormone-therapy users healthier than non-users even if the therapy itself did nothing for the heart.

This lesson gives you a vocabulary for that kind of error and a toolkit for avoiding it. The goal is not to make you an econometrician. It is to let you ask the one question that matters about any causal claim — compared with what? — and to judge whether the answer is credible.

understand.text: Causal effects are counterfactual comparisons

The effect of a training program on an employee is the difference between her performance with the program and her performance, at the same time, without it. One of those two outcomes is always missing: this is sometimes called the fundamental problem of causal inference. Every causal method is a strategy for filling in the missing counterfactual with a comparison group. The quality of the estimate is the quality of that substitute.

A naive comparison of participants with non-participants equals the true average effect *plus* selection bias: the difference the two groups would have shown even without the program. If motivated employees volunteer for training, the naive comparison credits the program with their motivation.
Three ways a correlation misleads

understand.caption: Confounders, mediators and colliders
rows: Z causes both X and Y
Adjust for Z, or use a design that breaks the Z→X link
Health consciousness drives both hormone-therapy use and heart health.
X causes M, which causes Y
Do not adjust for M if you want the total effect of X
A coaching program improves confidence, which improves sales; controlling for confidence hides the program’s effect.
X and Y both cause C
Do not select on or adjust for C; it creates a spurious association
Among start-ups that received venture funding, founders’ technical skill and charisma look negatively related, because either could get a firm funded.
Establish timing; use designs with clear sequence
Struggling hospitals hire more consultants; consultants are not making them struggle.

understand.text: Causal diagrams, often called DAGs (directed acyclic graphs), make these structures explicit: draw arrows for what you believe causes what, then ask which paths between X and Y are causal and which are “back doors” through common causes. Adjusting for the right variables closes back doors; adjusting for the wrong ones (mediators and colliders) creates bias. The diagram does not prove your assumptions. It forces you to state them.
Randomized controlled trials

Random assignment makes treatment independent of everything else about the units, observed or not, so the comparison group is a valid counterfactual on average. That is why the hormone-therapy trial could overturn decades of observational evidence. Angrist and Pischke describe randomized trials as the benchmark against which other designs are judged, and the “credibility revolution” in empirical economics as a shift toward research designs that mimic randomization ([Angrist & Pischke, 2010](R-angrist-2010-credibility); [Angrist & Pischke, 2014](R-angrist-2014-mastering)).
Natural experiments and quasi-experimental designs

When randomization is impossible, unethical or too slow, the next best thing is a situation in which something other than the units’ own choices determined who was treated. Four designs cover most of what you will read.

understand.caption: Four designs, one assumption each
rows: A coin decides who is treated
Randomization was carried out properly and people stayed in their groups
Compare the change in a treated group with the change in an untreated group
Parallel trends: without treatment both groups would have changed by the same amount
Different pre-trends; other shocks hitting one group
Compare units just above and just below a cutoff that determines treatment
Nothing else jumps at the cutoff and units cannot precisely sort around it
Manipulation of the running variable; effects only local to the cutoff
Use a factor that shifts treatment but affects the outcome only through treatment
Exclusion restriction: the instrument has no other path to the outcome
Weak instruments; hidden paths; effect applies only to those the instrument moves

understand.text: Angrist and Pischke teach each design through a real study. To illustrate regression discontinuity they use the U.S. minimum legal drinking age: death rates of young adults jump at the 21st birthday, when legal drinking begins, and people just under and just over 21 are otherwise nearly identical. For instrumental variables they use lotteries for oversubscribed charter schools, in which winning the lottery changes the chance of attending but should not otherwise affect test scores. For difference-in-differences they use the different policies of two Federal Reserve districts that split the state of Mississippi during the bank failures of 1930 ([Angrist & Pischke, 2014](R-angrist-2014-mastering)).

The most famous difference-in-differences study in economics compared fast-food employment in New Jersey, which raised its minimum wage in 1992, with neighboring eastern Pennsylvania, which did not. Using telephone surveys before and after the increase, Card and Krueger found no relative decline in New Jersey employment, challenging the textbook prediction ([Card & Krueger, 1994](R-card-1994-minimum)).

steps.label: Treated before
steps.text: Clinics adopting a new triage protocol: 52-minute average wait

steps.label: Treated after
steps.text: 44 minutes: a change of −8

steps.label: Comparison before / after
steps.text: Similar clinics without the protocol: 50 to 47, a change of −3

steps.label: Estimate

blocks.text: A *correlation* measures how closely two variables move together, from −1 to +1. A *regression* estimates how much one variable changes, on average, with another while holding a list of other variables constant — “controlling for” them. Controlling for a variable removes bias only if that variable is a confounder, is measured well, and the list includes every important confounder. Unmeasured confounders, such as motivation or health consciousness, are untouched by any regression. That is why “we controlled for 40 variables” is not, by itself, reassuring: what matters is whether the variables that drive both treatment and outcome are among them.

understand.title: Methodological note: what each design actually estimates

blocks.text: Designs differ not only in credibility but in *whose* effect they estimate. A randomized trial estimates the average effect among the kind of people enrolled. Regression discontinuity estimates the effect for units near the cutoff, which may differ from units far from it. Instrumental variables estimate the effect for “compliers” — those whose treatment status was changed by the instrument, such as families who attend a charter school only because they won the lottery. Difference-in-differences estimates the effect for the treated group under its specific circumstances. Each answer is valid for a particular population; none is automatically the effect for the population you care about. When a study is used to justify a policy for a different group, the gap between these populations is the generalization risk examined in [Lesson 4](#w04-l4).

challenge.text: Quasi-experimental designs can be attacked through their measurement and their assumptions, and the minimum-wage study shows how. Neumark and Wascher re-estimated the New Jersey effect using payroll records from restaurants instead of telephone survey answers and found employment declines ([Neumark & Wascher, 2000](R-neumark-2000-minimum)). Card and Krueger, whose original survey-based estimate had shown no relative decline ([Card & Krueger, 1994](R-card-1994-minimum)), replied in the same journal issue with other administrative data and again found small or no effects. The broader minimum-wage literature remains contested. The executive lesson is not which side won but that a credible design is necessary and not sufficient: outcome measurement, sample construction and the comparison group all remain open to challenge.

Even randomized trials have critics. Deaton and Cartwright argue that randomization balances confounders only in expectation, that trials estimate averages that can hide who is helped and who is harmed, and that a trial’s result says little about other settings without an understanding of why it worked ([Deaton & Cartwright, 2018](R-deaton-2018-understanding)). Defenders of design-based research respond that these are reasons to run better and more varied trials, not reasons to prefer weaker designs ([Angrist & Pischke, 2010](R-angrist-2010-credibility)).

There is also a limit on what designs can answer. Many executive questions — should we enter this market, should we reorganize the department — are one-off decisions where no comparison group exists. Causal reasoning still helps by forcing you to state the counterfactual and the mechanism, but you should be suspicious of anyone who claims the precision of an experiment for a decision that could never have one.

challenge.title: Executive twist: two credible analyses, opposite answers

blocks.text: A state education agency evaluates a tutoring program. One analyst uses difference-in-differences with schools that adopted later as the comparison and finds a meaningful gain. Another uses a regression discontinuity at the poverty threshold that determined eligibility and finds nothing. Both are competent. They may both be right: the discontinuity estimates the effect for schools near the threshold, where needs are moderate, while the difference-in-differences estimate is dominated by the poorest schools. Before choosing between them, ask whose effect each estimates, check whether pre-trends were parallel, and decide which population your funding decision concerns.

apply.text: A practical design ladder for organizational questions, from strongest to weakest, under typical constraints:

items: **Randomize** when the decision is repeated, reversible and the treatment can be rationed: training slots, software rollouts, outreach scripts, scheduling policies. If not everyone can be served at once, random order is fair and informative.
**Stagger** rollouts and choose the order at random, which converts a normal launch into a set of comparisons.
**Exploit a cutoff** that already determines treatment — a score threshold for a program, an age rule, a budget formula — and compare units just on either side.
**Use difference-in-differences** when one unit adopts a policy and comparable units do not; show pre-trends.
**Adjust for observed confounders** only as a last resort, state which unmeasured confounders could remain, and say how strong they would need to be to explain the result.

apply.text: In player development, selection and collider bias are everywhere. Players who receive extra biomechanics sessions are often those staff already believe in; comparing them with others confounds the sessions with that belief. Players who reach the major leagues are a filtered sample, so relationships observed only among major leaguers — for example between a physical tool and a skill — can be artifacts of the filter, the collider structure in the table above. A department that wants causal answers can randomize the order in which affiliates adopt a new program, use eligibility rules (such as age or service thresholds) as discontinuities, and pre-register a comparison with players who were similar before the program started.

Other industries show the same moves. Technology firms randomize product changes at scale. Governments use lotteries when demand for a program exceeds supply. Hospitals compare units that adopt a protocol early with those that adopt late. Militaries test doctrine in exercises that assign units to conditions. In each case the design question — what is the comparison, and why is it credible? — comes before the statistics.

Worked problem: a bank introduces a fraud-detection rule for all transactions above $5,000. Six months later, losses on transactions just above $5,000 are much lower than on transactions just below. Which design is this, what is its key assumption, and what behavior by fraudsters would threaten it? (Regression discontinuity; nothing else changes at $5,000; fraudsters who learn the threshold and split transactions to stay just below it would sort around the cutoff and bias the comparison.)

retain.text: A causal effect is a comparison with an unobserved counterfactual, so every estimate is only as good as its comparison group. Confounding, selection and collider bias make naive correlations misleading. Randomization solves them by design; difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity and instrumental variables can work when randomization cannot, each under one assumption you should ask to see defended.
For each of the four designs, state its key assumption in one sentence.
Give an example of a collider from your own field and explain the spurious correlation it would create.
Why did the randomized hormone-therapy trial disagree with earlier observational studies?

takeaways: Every causal claim is a comparison with a counterfactual; ask what the comparison group was.
Confounders should be adjusted for; mediators and colliders should not.
Randomization balances unobserved confounders by design and is the benchmark for other designs.

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: a city introduces a congestion charge in its downtown district in January. An analyst compares the change in bus ridership downtown from the year before to the year after with the change over the same period in a similar city without a charge.

check.explanation: Comparing before-after changes in a treated and an untreated unit is difference-in-differences. Its key assumption is that, without the charge, both cities’ ridership would have moved in parallel; a new bus line or an economic shock in one city would violate it.

optionFeedback.a: There is no cutoff on a running variable here; the comparison is across cities over time.
optionFeedback.c: No instrument is used; the charge is the treatment itself.
optionFeedback.d: Nothing was randomized; the city chose to adopt the charge.

check.prompt: What is the main flaw in this reasoning?

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: “Among the 300 professionals our firm promoted to partner over the last decade, those with the strongest technical ratings had the weakest client-relationship ratings. So technical excellence must undermine relationship skills.”

options.text: Reverse causation: weak relationships cause people to invest in technical skills.
Collider bias: promotion depends on both traits, so selecting only promoted partners can create a negative correlation even if the traits are unrelated in the population.
Regression to the mean in the ratings.
The sample of 300 is too small to detect a correlation.

check.explanation: Promotion is caused by both technical and relationship strength. Among promoted people, someone weak on one trait must have been strong on the other to be promoted, which induces a negative correlation. This is collider (selection) bias; the population correlation could be zero or positive.

optionFeedback.a: Possible in principle, but the selection structure produces the pattern without any causal story at all.
optionFeedback.c: Regression to the mean concerns repeated measurement of extremes, not the correlation between two traits in a selected group.
optionFeedback.d: The problem is who is in the sample, not how many.

lessons.title: Reading a Study Like a Skeptic
lessons.summary: A credible design is not enough: you must also judge the size of the effect, the validity of the measures, the population studied, and whether the metric still means what it used to.
objectives: Translate a standardized effect size into practical terms and judge whether it matters.
Diagnose measurement problems — low reliability, poor validity and metric gaming — and predict their effect on conclusions.
Assess external validity and survivorship in a study before applying it to your organization.
lessons.executive: Before acting on a study, ask four questions. How big is the effect, in units you care about, with what uncertainty? Does the measure capture the thing you care about, reliably, and would it still do so if people were rewarded on it? Were the people and settings studied like yours, and did the sample include the failures as well as the survivors? Is the mechanism likely to operate in your context? Significance answers none of these. A huge sample can make a trivial effect significant; a noisy measure can hide a real one; and a metric that becomes a target can stop measuring anything.

explore.text: A large online retailer reports that a redesigned product page increased average time on page by a statistically significant margin, p < .001, in a test with two million visitors. The vice president of product wants to roll it out globally. A data scientist points out that the estimated increase is 0.4 seconds and that revenue per visitor did not change. The scenario is hypothetical; the confusion between significance and importance is not.
Before reading on: list the questions you would ask before approving the rollout. Which of them could the p-value answer?

Lessons 1 to 3 asked whether an effect is real and causal. This lesson asks the questions that remain even when the answer is yes: is it big enough to matter, is it measured properly, and will it travel to your setting?

understand.text: Effect size: how big, in units that matter

An *effect size* expresses magnitude. Standardized measures such as Cohen’s *d* (the difference between groups in standard-deviation units) or a correlation *r* allow comparison across studies; raw measures (minutes, dollars, percentage points) allow judgment about consequences. Always ask for both, and for the confidence interval around them. A *d* of 0.2 means the average treated unit sits at roughly the 58th percentile of the comparison group — noticeable in aggregate, invisible in most individuals.

Funder and Ozer argue that the conventional labels small, medium and large are close to meaningless without context. Small effects can be highly consequential when they accumulate over many occasions or apply to many people, and very large effects reported from small studies are more likely to be overestimates than discoveries. They recommend judging effects against well-understood benchmarks and against their practical consequences ([Funder & Ozer, 2019](R-funder-2019-evaluating)).

Sample size and effect size are independent questions. With two million visitors, an effect of 0.4 seconds can be estimated precisely and declared significant; that tells you it is probably not zero, not that it is worth anything. Conversely, a pilot with forty participants may show an effect large enough to matter that is not significant because the interval is wide. The executive translation is: significance is about detectability; importance is about magnitude, cost and consequence.

understand.caption: Significance versus importance
cells: Probably nothing worth pursuing, or a study too small to tell — check the interval
Real but trivial: common with very large samples; do not confuse precision with value
Possibly important but uncertain: buy more information if the decision allows
Worth acting on, if the design and measures hold up
understand.note: Original APERTURE matrix. The y-axis refers to the point estimate in practical units.

understand.text: Measurement: reliability, validity and attenuation

*Reliability* is consistency: would the measure give the same answer if repeated? *Validity* is meaning: does it measure what you claim? A bathroom scale that is always five pounds light is reliable but not valid. A supervisor rating that varies with the supervisor’s mood is neither. Low reliability has a specific, predictable consequence: random error in a measure shrinks observed correlations and effects toward zero, a phenomenon known as *attenuation*. If an outcome has reliability 0.4, a true effect of 0.4 standard deviations shows up as roughly 0.25, and a study powered for the true effect will often miss it. Unreliable measures therefore produce false negatives and, combined with a significance filter, erratic estimates.

Validity failures are worse because they are not random. A measure can correlate with the target in ordinary conditions and still fail as a guide when conditions change. Validity has to be argued for: what does the measure capture, what does it miss, and what else moves it?

Measurement can even manufacture a famous finding. For three decades, the “hot hand” in basketball was a textbook example of a cognitive illusion. Miller and Sanjurjo proved that the standard way of measuring streaks — the proportion of hits immediately following a run of hits within finite sequences — is biased downward, so a shooter with no streakiness would appear anti-streaky. Correcting the bias reversed the conclusion of the original controlled-shooting analysis ([Miller & Sanjurjo, 2018](R-miller-2018-surprised)). How large the hot hand is in game conditions remains debated.
Goodhart and Campbell: when the measure becomes the target

Donald Campbell stated the principle now called Campbell’s law: the more a quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more it is subject to corruption pressures and the more it distorts the processes it was meant to monitor ([Campbell, 1979](R-campbell-1979-assessing)). The economist Charles Goodhart made a parallel observation about monetary targets, usually paraphrased as “when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure”. Both are principles distilled from experience rather than laws demonstrated by systematic studies, but they predict a recurring pattern: hospitals that are rewarded for short waiting times reclassify when the clock starts; schools rewarded on pass rates focus on students near the threshold; sales teams rewarded on bookings pull revenue forward.
External validity and survivorship

*External validity* is whether a result holds for other people, places and times. Deaton and Cartwright argue that a well-run trial establishes that a program worked *there*; using it *here* requires knowing why it worked and whether the supporting conditions are present ([Deaton & Cartwright, 2018](R-deaton-2018-understanding)). Results from volunteers, single firms, laboratory tasks or another country are not wrong; they are local until shown otherwise.

*Survivorship bias* arises when the sample includes only units that passed some filter. Databases of mutual funds that drop closed funds overstate average returns; studies of “habits of successful companies” sample only firms that survived; analysis of veteran employees ignores those who left. Ask what happened to the cases that are not in the data and whether their absence is related to the outcome.

understand.title: Prerequisite: standard deviation and standardized effects

blocks.text: The *standard deviation* measures how spread out individual values are around their average; in roughly bell-shaped data, about two thirds of cases lie within one standard deviation of the mean. A standardized effect divides a difference by the standard deviation, so *d* = 0.5 means the groups differ by half a typical spread. Standardization makes effects comparable across measures but hides practical meaning: half a standard deviation of patient satisfaction and half a standard deviation of mortality are not equally important. Convert back to natural units before deciding.

understand.title: Methodological note: correcting for attenuation, and its dangers

blocks.text: Psychometrics offers a correction: divide an observed correlation by the square root of the product of the two measures’ reliabilities to estimate the correlation between the underlying true scores. It is a useful thought experiment — it tells you how much signal the noise may be hiding — but it is easy to abuse. Reliability estimates are themselves uncertain, the correction can produce implausible values above 1, and it describes a relationship between idealized constructs that no one can act on directly. Decisions are made on measured quantities. Improving the measure usually beats correcting for it.

challenge.text: Skepticism has its own failure modes. An executive who can find a threat to validity in every study can justify ignoring any evidence that is inconvenient, which is motivated reasoning dressed as rigor. Every study has limitations; the question is whether a specific limitation is plausible and large enough to change the decision. A useful discipline is to state, for each criticism, which direction it would bias the result and roughly how much.

Second, the small-effects argument cuts both ways. Funder and Ozer show why small effects can matter at scale ([Funder & Ozer, 2019](R-funder-2019-evaluating)), but it is also common for advocates to invoke scale to rescue effects that are uncertain as well as small. A small effect is worth acting on when it is well established, cheap to obtain and applied many times; a small, uncertain, expensive effect is not.

Third, external validity is sometimes better than critics suggest. Mechanisms grounded in basic physiology, economics or cognition often travel well. The burden is to argue from mechanism, not to assume either universality or uniqueness. “Our organization is different” is true and, by itself, uninformative.

apply.text: Player development offers a dense set of examples. Effect sizes: a new strength program that adds a fraction of a mile per hour to average fastball velocity may be real and still be small relative to its cost in time and injury risk, or it may compound over a career. Reliability: many short-sample performance metrics have low reliability, so a well-designed program judged on them over a few weeks will often look ineffective. Goodhart: if coaches are evaluated on players’ bat-speed gains, practice may drift toward the specific drills that move bat speed rather than toward game performance. External validity: a technology validated on college athletes in a laboratory may not transfer to professional athletes in competition. Survivorship: studying the development paths of established major leaguers tells you little about which paths fail.

apply.title: Executive twist: the vendor’s white paper

blocks.text: A vendor presents a white paper showing that firms using its analytics platform grew revenue 18% faster than non-users. The sample is customers who renewed; the comparison is the industry average; the outcome period begins after adoption. You have a renewal decision and a board that likes the number. You need not prove the claim false. You can name the specific threats — selection of growing firms into adoption, survivorship among renewals, no pre-adoption comparison — and ask for a design that addresses them: a comparison with firms that trialed and did not adopt, with pre-adoption trends shown. A vendor confident in its product should welcome that request.

check.prompt: A trial with 400,000 customers finds that a new billing reminder reduces late payments by 0.1 percentage points (95% CI 0.05 to 0.15; p < .001). Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The effect is large because the p-value is very small.
The effect is real with high probability but small; whether it is worth adopting depends on its cost and the value of 0.1 points at scale.
The effect is too small to be real.
The confidence interval is too wide to draw any conclusion.

check.explanation: The narrow interval excluding zero indicates a real but small effect. Whether it is worth adopting is an economic question: a nearly free reminder applied to millions of bills may be worthwhile even at 0.1 points; an expensive one may not.

optionFeedback.a: A small p-value reflects detectability, driven here by the huge sample, not magnitude.
optionFeedback.c: Small and real are compatible; the interval excludes zero.
optionFeedback.d: The interval is narrow: 0.05 to 0.15 points.

check.prompt: A school district starts ranking principals on the share of students who score just above the proficiency cut. Within two years, proficiency rates rise but scores of the highest- and lowest-achieving students stagnate. Which principle best explains the pattern?

options.text: Regression to the mean.
Campbell’s law: an indicator used for high-stakes decisions distorts the process it monitors.
Attenuation due to low reliability.
Collider bias.

check.explanation: Rewarding a threshold indicator encourages effort on students near the threshold at the expense of others, so the indicator improves while the underlying goal does not. This is the distortion Campbell and Goodhart described.

optionFeedback.c: Attenuation shrinks observed effects; it does not explain strategic behavior.
optionFeedback.d: No selection on a common effect is involved.

lessons.title: Evidence Hierarchies, Meta-Analysis and Their Limits
lessons.summary: Hierarchies of evidence are useful defaults, not verdicts; meta-analyses inherit the biases of what they combine, and good judgment weighs design, consistency, mechanism and prior knowledge together.
objectives: Explain the logic of evidence hierarchies and identify cases where a lower-ranked design deserves more weight.
Interpret a meta-analysis, including heterogeneity and publication bias.
Combine several imperfect lines of evidence into a stated degree of belief that would change with specific new information.
lessons.executive: Evidence pyramids rank designs by their typical protection against bias: systematic reviews and randomized trials at the top, cohort and case-control studies in the middle, expert opinion at the bottom. That ranking is a sensible default and a poor substitute for judgment. A meta-analysis of small, biased studies can be confidently wrong; a large effect with an obvious mechanism may need no trial; and a well-run trial elsewhere may not apply to you. Weigh design, size, consistency, mechanism and relevance together, state your degree of belief, and say what evidence would change it.

explore.text: In 2003 the BMJ published a systematic review of randomized controlled trials of parachutes for preventing death in people jumping from aircraft. It found none, and concluded — tongue in cheek — that the effectiveness of parachutes had not been subjected to rigorous evaluation, suggesting that advocates of evidence-based medicine might volunteer for a trial ([Smith & Pell, 2003](R-smith-2003-parachute)). The satire made a serious point: a rigid hierarchy that demands randomized evidence for everything can be absurd when an effect is enormous and its mechanism obvious.

Before reading on: think of an intervention in your field that everyone believes works without randomized evidence. Is it more like a parachute (huge effect, obvious mechanism) or more like hormone therapy (modest effect, plausible story, strong selection)?

This final lesson pulls the week together. You have seen how noise, flexible analysis, weak designs, poor measures and selective publication can mislead. Now the task is to decide what to believe when the evidence is mixed, which is the normal condition of executive work.

understand.text: The ordering is a ranking of *typical* protection against bias, not a ranking of truth. It answers the question “which design, other things equal, is less likely to mislead about a causal effect?” Other things are rarely equal. Medicine’s more mature grading systems therefore adjust ratings up or down for risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness and publication bias, and upward for very large effects or dose-response relationships. You can use the same logic informally.

In practice, five questions move a piece of evidence up or down from its starting rank. Is the effect large relative to plausible bias? A tenfold difference is hard to explain by confounding; a ten percent difference is easy. Is there a dose-response pattern, with more exposure producing more effect? Do studies with different designs and different weaknesses agree? Is the evidence direct — the same population, intervention and outcome you care about — or indirect? And is it precise enough to distinguish an effect that matters from one that does not? A large, consistent, direct observational literature can deserve more weight than one small, indirect trial; a randomized trial with heavy attrition can deserve less than its rank suggests.
Meta-analysis: what pooling can and cannot do

A *meta-analysis* combines estimates from several studies, weighting each by its precision, to produce a summary effect with a narrower interval than any single study. Its great strength is reducing random error. It also lets you examine *heterogeneity* — whether studies disagree more than chance would predict — and look for moderators that explain the disagreement. When heterogeneity is large, a single pooled number is a misleading summary: the question becomes when and for whom the effect occurs.

Pooling cannot remove bias that every included study shares. If small studies with null results went unpublished, the meta-analysis averages a filtered sample. Kvarven, Strømland and Johannesson compared meta-analyses with large preregistered multi-laboratory replications of the same psychological effects and found that meta-analytic estimates were substantially larger, on average roughly three times the replication estimates; common bias-correction methods reduced but did not eliminate the gap ([Kvarven et al., 2020](R-kvarven-2020-comparing)).

understand.text: Bayesian updating: combining lines of evidence

Bayesian reasoning offers a disciplined way to combine evidence. Start with a prior belief based on base rates, mechanism and earlier studies. Each new piece of evidence shifts the belief in proportion to how much more likely it would be if the claim were true than if it were false — its *likelihood ratio*. Strong designs with large samples have large likelihood ratios; weak, flexible studies have small ones, because they would often produce a positive result even if the claim were false. Independent lines of evidence that rely on different assumptions — a trial, a natural experiment, a mechanistic study, a dose-response pattern — are worth more together than several studies sharing one bias. This idea is sometimes called *triangulation*.

blocks.text: In a meta-analysis each study’s estimate is weighted by its precision, roughly the inverse of its squared standard error, so large studies count more. A *fixed-effect* model assumes all studies estimate one common effect. A *random-effects* model assumes the true effect varies across settings and estimates the average of that distribution, plus how much it varies. When studies genuinely differ, the random-effects average is the more honest summary, and the spread of true effects is often more decision-relevant than the average: it tells you how much the result could differ in your setting.

understand.title: Methodological note: detecting publication bias, and why detection is hard

blocks.text: A *funnel plot* graphs each study’s effect against its precision. Without bias, small studies scatter symmetrically around the pooled effect; with publication bias, small studies with small or negative effects are missing, leaving an asymmetric funnel. Statistical tests and corrections (such as trim-and-fill or regression-based approaches) try to quantify and adjust for the asymmetry. All have limits: asymmetry can arise from genuine heterogeneity, and corrections rely on assumptions about how the filter worked.

The comparison with preregistered replications suggests that corrections often leave meta-analytic estimates too high ([Kvarven et al., 2020](R-kvarven-2020-comparing)). The most reliable remedy is structural rather than statistical: registered studies and reports whose publication does not depend on results ([Scheel, Schijen & Lakens, 2021](R-scheel-2021-excess)).

challenge.text: Two critiques pull in opposite directions. Deaton and Cartwright argue that ranking designs encourages people to treat randomized results as the answer, when a trial establishes only an average effect in a particular population and says little about application elsewhere without understanding the mechanism ([Deaton & Cartwright, 2018](R-deaton-2018-understanding)). Advocates of design-based evidence respond that observational studies have repeatedly misled — hormone therapy is the canonical example — and that the hierarchy exists because intuitions about confounding are unreliable ([Rossouw et al., 2002](R-rossouw-2002-risks); [Angrist & Pischke, 2010](R-angrist-2010-credibility)). Both are right about different failure modes: one warns against over-trusting the top of the pyramid, the other against under-trusting it.

A second limit is that most organizational decisions never accumulate a literature. There will be no meta-analysis of your reorganization. Here the hierarchy is used differently: as a guide to which internal evidence to trust (a staggered rollout over a testimonial), and as a prompt to borrow priors from related fields while discounting for differences in context.

Finally, the parachute satire is often misused. It applies when effects are dramatic and mechanisms unambiguous. Most organizational and behavioral interventions have modest effects, plausible competing explanations and strong selection; for them, the lesson of hormone therapy is more relevant than the lesson of parachutes ([Smith & Pell, 2003](R-smith-2003-parachute)).

challenge.title: Executive twist: the meta-analysis versus your own data

blocks.text: A meta-analysis of 60 studies reports that a type of peer-mentoring program improves employee retention, with a modest pooled effect and substantial heterogeneity. Your own organization’s staggered rollout across four regions shows no effect, with a wide interval. Your head of people wants to scale the program because “60 studies can’t be wrong”; your CFO wants to cut it because “our data say it doesn’t work”. A better frame: the literature sets a prior that the program helps somewhere; the heterogeneity says context matters; your data are too imprecise to overturn the prior or confirm it. The decision should turn on cost, on whether your context resembles the studies where it worked, and on designing the next phase to be informative.

apply.text: A baseball operations department faces this problem constantly: published research from other sports and populations, vendor claims, internal analyses of varying quality, and coaches’ experience. A practical evidence-grading routine for a development decision might look like this:

items: State the claim precisely, including the population (for example, “for pitchers aged 18–22 at the lowest levels”).
List each line of evidence with its design, sample, outcome measure and relevance to that population.
Rate each line’s risk of bias and its directness, using the hierarchy as a starting point and adjusting for size, consistency and mechanism.
Write a one-sentence posterior: “We believe the effect is probably positive and modest; we would be surprised by an effect larger than X.”
Name the decision rule and the evidence that would change it, and build that evidence-gathering into the rollout.

apply.text: Healthcare uses structured versions of this routine in guideline development; government agencies use evidence clearinghouses that rate programs by design quality; consulting and finance teams use investment memos that separate facts, estimates and assumptions. The common thread is transparency about why some evidence counts more.

Internal evidence deserves the same grading. A department’s own data are the most relevant evidence it has and often the most biased: programs are usually started where problems were worst (inviting regression to the mean), offered to the most willing participants (inviting selection) and judged by the people who championed them. Relevance does not excuse design. The practical consequence is to build the comparison into the program from the start — random or staggered order, a pre-specified outcome, a record of every pilot — so that internal evidence can earn the weight its relevance promises.

takeaways: Hierarchies rank typical protection against bias, not truth; adjust for size, consistency, mechanism and relevance.
Meta-analyses reduce chance but inherit shared bias; preregistered replications often find much smaller effects.
Large heterogeneity means “it depends” is the finding; ask for the spread, not just the average.
Bayesian updating combines lines of evidence; independent designs with different weaknesses are worth most together.
For decisions, state a degree of belief, a plausible range, and what would change your mind.

check.prompt: A meta-analysis pools 25 small studies, almost all statistically significant, and reports a precise, moderate pooled effect. Which concern is most important?

options.text: Pooling 25 studies always produces a biased estimate.
If non-significant studies went unpublished, the pooled estimate inherits that filter and is likely too large despite its precision.
The pooled estimate is imprecise because each study is small.
Meta-analyses cannot include small studies.

check.explanation: A literature of small studies that are almost all significant is a classic signature of a significance filter. Pooling reduces random error, so the estimate looks precise, but it cannot remove a bias that all the included studies share.

optionFeedback.a: Pooling is not inherently biased; the problem is what was available to pool.
optionFeedback.c: Pooling many small studies produces a precise estimate; precision is not the problem.
optionFeedback.d: Small studies are routinely included, weighted by precision.

check.prompt: You think there is a 20% chance a new onboarding program reduces early attrition. A pilot result arrives that is three times as likely if the program works as if it does not (likelihood ratio 3). What is your updated probability that the program works, in percent?
check.working: Prior odds = 0.2 / 0.8 = 0.25. Posterior odds = 0.25 × 3 = 0.75. Probability = 0.75 / 1.75 ≈ 0.429, about 43%.
check.explanation: Convert the prior to odds, multiply by the likelihood ratio, and convert back. A moderately informative result moves a skeptical prior a long way, but not to certainty: the program is still more likely not to work than to work.
