glossary.definition: The tendency of cases selected for extreme values on a noisy measure to be closer to the average when measured again, with or without any intervention.
The consistency of a measure: the share of its variation that reflects stable differences rather than noise. Low reliability attenuates observed effects.
The degree to which a measure captures the construct it claims to measure, and supports the inferences drawn from it.
A range produced by a procedure that captures the true value in a stated share of repeated samples (for example 95%); read as the effect sizes reasonably compatible with the data.
The probability of data at least as extreme as those observed if a specified model, usually of no effect, were true. Not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
The probability that a study detects a true effect of a given size at its significance threshold; it rises with sample size, effect size and measurement precision.

glossary.term: Type M and type S errors
glossary.definition: A type M error is an exaggerated estimate of an effect’s magnitude; a type S error is an estimate with the wrong sign. Both are common among significant results from low-powered studies.
The many analytic choices (outcomes, samples, covariates, stopping rules) that, when made after seeing the data, inflate false positives.
The selective publication or presentation of results depending on their significance or direction, which distorts the visible body of evidence.
A time-stamped plan specifying hypotheses, outcomes and analyses before data are collected or seen.
A publication format in which a journal reviews and accepts a study’s question and design before results exist, so publication does not depend on the outcome.
The outcome that would have occurred for the same units without the treatment; every causal effect compares an observed outcome with a counterfactual.
A variable that influences both the treatment and the outcome, creating an association that is not the treatment’s effect.
A variable caused by both the treatment and the outcome (or their causes); selecting on or adjusting for it creates a spurious association.
A design that compares the change over time in a treated group with the change in an untreated group, assuming their trends would otherwise have been parallel.
A design that compares units just above and just below a cutoff that determines treatment.
A factor that changes the likelihood of treatment but affects the outcome only through the treatment, such as a lottery for program slots.
Whether a result obtained in one population, setting and time holds in others.
The principle that an indicator used as a target or for high-stakes decisions tends to be gamed and to lose its value as a measure.
A statistical synthesis that pools estimates from several studies, weighted by precision, and examines how much they vary (heterogeneity).

exercise.title: Evidence Lab

intro.text: The Evidence Lab simulates thousands of two-group studies of the same question, each with its own random sample. You control the true effect, the sample size per group, how many outcomes each “researcher” measures (and reports only the best), whether only significant results get published, and how reliable the outcome measure is. The lab then shows what a reader of that literature would see.

Work through the seven presets in order. Each describes a fictional study from a different industry. Before you run a preset, write down your prediction in your notebook; after the run, compare it with the result and read the lesson. Then change one parameter at a time and predict again. The point is to build intuition you can use when a single study lands on your desk.

items: **Share significant**: how often studies reach p < .05. With a true effect this is power; with no effect it is the false-positive rate.
**Exaggeration ratio**: the average estimate among significant results divided by the true effect (type-M error).
**Sign errors**: significant results pointing the wrong way (type-S error).
**A single study**: one random draw, which is all a real decision-maker usually sees.

presets.title: A promising pilot
presets.story: Fictional: a software company pilots a peer-coaching program for new engineers. Twenty engineers per group; the true improvement in ninety-day productivity is modest (d = 0.3). Only pilots with significant results are presented to the leadership team.
presets.predict: Before you run it: what share of these pilots will reach p < .05, and how large will the average effect be among the pilots that leadership actually sees?

key.lesson: Only about one pilot in six or seven reaches significance, and those that do report an average effect of roughly 0.75–0.8 — about two and a half times the true 0.3. Leadership sees only the lucky draws. Low power plus a significance filter does not just miss effects; it exaggerates the ones it shows you (type-M error).

presets.title: The well-powered replication
presets.story: Fictional: a hospital network repeats a discharge-checklist study with 250 patients per group. The true effect on a readmission-risk score is the same modest d = 0.3. All results are reported.
presets.predict: Before you run it: compared with the pilot in preset 1, how often will the study be significant, and how close will significant estimates be to the truth?

key.lesson: Roughly nine studies in ten are significant, and significant estimates average close to 0.3. When power is high, the significance filter barely distorts the estimate. The same true effect looks modest and reliable here and dramatic and fragile in preset 1: the difference is design, not reality.

presets.title: Ten outcomes, no effect
presets.story: Fictional: a bank evaluates a financial-wellness app for employees with 40 people per group. The app has no effect on anything. The evaluation team measures ten outcomes (stress, absences, savings rate, engagement and so on) and highlights whichever looks best.
presets.predict: Before you run it: the true effect is zero. What share of evaluations will report a significant benefit on at least one outcome?

key.lesson: About 40% of evaluations find a “significant” result even though the app does nothing, because ten chances at 5% add up (1 − 0.95^10 ≈ 0.40 when outcomes are independent; somewhat less when they are correlated). This is undisclosed multiple testing, one of the researcher degrees of freedom in Lesson 2. Set outcomes back to 1 and the rate returns to about 5%.

presets.title: The noisy ruler
presets.story: Fictional: a school district tests a teacher-coaching program with 100 teachers per group. The true effect on teaching quality is solid (d = 0.4), but quality is measured with a classroom-observation rubric whose reliability is only 0.4.
presets.predict: Before you run it: with a perfect measure this design detects the effect about 80% of the time. What happens to the detection rate and the average estimate with this rubric?

key.lesson: The observed effect shrinks to about 0.25 (0.4 × √0.4), and only about 43% of studies reach significance. A real program would often be judged a failure because of the ruler, not the program. Raise reliability to 1.0 to compare. Measurement quality is a design decision with the same consequences as sample size.

presets.title: Big data, tiny effect
presets.story: Fictional: a government benefits agency tests a redesigned letter with 500 recipients per group (the lab’s maximum; real agencies often test far more). The true effect on on-time form completion is small (d = 0.15).
presets.predict: Before you run it: will most studies be significant? If so, does that make the letter important?

key.lesson: A majority of studies (around two in three) are significant, and estimates cluster tightly around 0.15. Larger samples would make significance nearly certain. Significance here means the effect is probably not zero; whether 0.15 standard deviations is worth a redesign depends on cost and scale. Detectability and importance are separate questions (Lesson 4).

presets.title: The file drawer
presets.story: Fictional: legal-aid organizations run many small evaluations (30 clients per group) of a court-reminder service whose true effect on appearance rates is tiny (d = 0.1). Only significant results get written up, and a reviewer later summarizes the published literature.
presets.predict: Before you run it: what average effect will the published literature show, and will any published results point in the wrong direction?

key.lesson: Fewer than one study in ten is significant. The published positive results average around 0.5 — roughly five times the truth — and a noticeable minority of significant results (on the order of one in seven) have the wrong sign. A meta-analysis of this literature would be precise and badly wrong (Lesson 5). Turn the publication filter off to see the honest picture.

presets.title: The drill that worked
presets.story: Fictional professional application: a player-development staff tests a new hitting drill with 15 players per group over a few weeks. The drill truly helps (d = 0.4), but short-sample batted-ball metrics have reliability around 0.5, and the analyst checks four metrics and reports the best.
presets.predict: Before you run it: three problems are combined — small samples, a noisy measure, and four outcomes. Predict the share significant and the average significant estimate.

key.lesson: Roughly two studies in five reach significance, but mostly by picking the luckiest of four noisy metrics; significant estimates average around 0.85, about double the true effect and triple what the measure can actually register. Set outcomes to 1 and power collapses to about 13%. The drill really works, yet almost every individual study either misses it or exaggerates it. The remedy is larger, pre-specified, more reliable evaluations — for example pooling cohorts across affiliates.

debrief.text: The lab shows that the reliability of a body of evidence can be predicted from its design: power, measurement reliability, the number of outcomes examined and the publication filter. The same true effect can produce a literature that looks dramatic and fragile or modest and solid. Exaggerated effects, false positives and missed effects are not signs of bad luck; they are the expected output of particular designs.

The lab does not show everything. It models honest random sampling with independent outcomes, normally distributed data and a single two-group comparison. It does not model confounding, selection into treatment, fraud, heterogeneous effects, correlated outcomes, or optional stopping. Real studies combine these problems with the ones simulated here. Treat the numbers as teaching approximations, not as estimates for any real literature.

assumptions: Each simulated study compares two independent groups of equal size n with normally distributed outcomes and a two-sided test at p < .05.
The true standardized effect (Cohen’s d) is the same in every study; there is no heterogeneity across settings.
When outcomes > 1, the outcomes are simulated as independent and the study reports the outcome with the strongest result, modeling undisclosed multiple testing.
Reliability below 1 attenuates the observable effect by the square root of reliability.
With the publication filter on, only significant results are shown in the published histogram and averages.

case.title: The Executive Disagreement
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional. Numbers are synthetic and constructed for teaching.

body.text: Grace Albright had been chief executive of Tamsin River Health for eleven months when the heart-failure question reached her desk in the form of two memos that reached opposite conclusions from the same spreadsheet. Tamsin River operates five hospitals across a mixed urban and rural region. Heart failure is its most common cause of readmission, and readmissions matter twice: patients who return within thirty days are sicker and more frightened, and the system’s largest commercial payer had announced that, starting next fiscal year, it would withhold part of its payments from hospitals with high readmission rates.

Two years earlier, the chief nursing officer, Dr. Teresa Valdivia, had launched a transitional-care program called Bridge Home at the two hospitals with the worst heart-failure readmission rates, Northgate and Riverside. Bridge Home assigns a nurse navigator to each enrolled patient before discharge, schedules a home visit within seventy-two hours, reconciles medications, and follows up by phone for four weeks. Enrollment is voluntary; navigators offer it to eligible patients, and roughly 57% accept. The program costs about $1.1 million a year across the two hospitals, mostly navigator salaries.

The board’s quality committee meets in three weeks. Grace must bring a recommendation: expand Bridge Home to the other three hospitals at an added cost of about $1.6 million a year, keep it where it is, or do something else.
Dr. Valdivia’s memo

Valdivia’s memo was short and confident. In the year before Bridge Home began, the two program hospitals had a heart-failure readmission rate of 24.5%. In the most recent year it was 19.8%, a drop of almost five points. The three other hospitals barely moved over the same period. Within the program hospitals, the contrast was even sharper: enrolled patients were readmitted at 14.1%, against 23.9% for eligible patients who declined. “Every month we wait,” she wrote, “patients at Lakeview, Eastfield and St. Brendan’s are readmitted who would not have been. The evidence is consistent across every cut of the data. The penalty is coming. We should expand now.”

Valdivia had built the program herself, recruited the navigators and knew many of the patients by name. She was respected across the system, and the nurses at the other three hospitals had been asking for months when Bridge Home would reach them.
Marcus Feld’s memo

The chief analytics officer, Marcus Feld, had joined Tamsin River from a health-insurance company a year earlier. His memo was longer and, in Valdivia’s view, unnecessarily cold. He did not dispute the numbers. He disputed what they meant.

First, he pointed out that Northgate and Riverside had been chosen because their readmission rates had spiked in the year before launch. Two years before launch their rate had been 22.0%, not 24.5%. “We selected the program hospitals on a bad year,” he wrote. “Some of the improvement is the bad year not repeating.” Measured against the earlier baseline and compared with the other three hospitals, he calculated a relative improvement of about 1.3 points rather than 4.7 or 3.5.

Second, he argued that the comparison of enrolled with non-enrolled patients said little about the program. Enrolled patients were more likely to have a family caregiver at home, less likely to be discharged to a skilled nursing facility, and more likely to have attended a cardiology follow-up in the previous year. “The patients who say yes are the patients who were going to do better anyway,” he wrote. “The ten-point gap is mostly who chose the program.”

Third, the same year Bridge Home launched, Northgate had opened a heart-failure clinic with extended hours, funded by a separate grant. Riverside had not. When Feld split the results, most of the improvement after the first year was at Northgate.

Feld did not recommend cancelling Bridge Home. He recommended expanding it to the other three hospitals in a randomized order — a stepped rollout in which each hospital’s start date is drawn by lot over eighteen months — and, within hospitals, randomly assigning the order in which units receive navigators. “We will reach every hospital within eighteen months,” he wrote, “and we will finally know what we are paying for. If the program works as well as Teresa believes, we will be able to show it to the payer and to the board.”
The conversation

Grace met the two of them together on a Thursday evening. Valdivia spoke first. “I understand the statistics,” she said. “But Marcus is asking us to deliberately delay a program for patients at three hospitals so that he can have a cleaner study. If we believe it works — and the nurses, the patients and the numbers all say it does — then randomizing the start dates means some patients get readmitted so we can be certain. I don’t think that’s ethical.”

Feld answered carefully. “We can’t staff all three hospitals at once anyway. Recruiting navigators takes months. Somebody has to go first. I’m only asking that we let a lottery decide the order instead of a meeting, and that we write down in advance what we’ll measure. And I’d push back on ‘we believe it works.’ We believe something worked at Northgate. We don’t know if it was Bridge Home.”
Valdivia shook her head. “The published literature on transitional care is positive. This is not a speculative idea.”

“It’s mixed,” Feld said. “The evidence team’s summary found effects ranging from nothing to large, and the two randomized trials in it were at the low end. The large effects come from before-after studies like ours.”

The chief financial officer, who had joined late, added a third consideration. The payer penalty would be calculated on the system’s overall readmission rate. If the true effect were near Valdivia’s estimate, expansion would more than pay for itself in avoided readmissions and penalties. If it were near Feld’s, expansion would cost more than it saved, though it might still be worth doing for patients. “I can live with either,” she said, “but I need to know which one I’m presenting.”
What Grace does not know

Grace noticed what neither memo could answer. Nobody had measured whether enrolled patients took their medications more reliably, the mechanism the program was designed to change. The navigators’ caseloads varied widely, and nobody knew whether outcomes varied with them. The three remaining hospitals differed from the first two: Lakeview was rural with long travel distances for home visits; St. Brendan’s served a large population of patients whose first language was neither English nor Spanish, the two languages in which Bridge Home operated. And the nurses at the other hospitals were already frustrated; a lottery might feel to them like being told their patients mattered less.

She also noticed something about her own reaction. She liked Valdivia’s program, and she liked Valdivia. She found Feld’s memo persuasive and slightly irritating. She wondered how much of her judgment was about the evidence and how much was about the people.

The board would ask a simple question: does Bridge Home work? Grace was beginning to think that the honest answer was “probably somewhat, and we have not been set up to know how much” — and that her real decision was not whether the program works, but what to do under that uncertainty, and how to make sure that a year from now the system knew more than it did today.

Assumptions: 2,400 eligible discharges per year at the three hospitals; $14,000 average cost per avoided readmission; the payer penalty could add roughly $0.6–1.0M a year if the system-wide rate is not reduced, but its exact formula has not been published. Patient benefit is not monetized.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 5 — Evidence team’s summary of external studies of similar programs
exhibits.note: Synthetic: a fictional evidence summary written for this case; no real studies are described. Assumptions: the team searched published and conference sources only.

assumptions: The three non-program hospitals can be staffed with navigators one at a time over about eighteen months regardless of the decision.
The payer penalty is based on the system-wide readmission rate; its exact formula is not yet known.
Bridge Home operates only in English and Spanish.
There is no evidence of harm from the program; the disagreement is about the size of its benefit.
Grace has authority to choose the rollout order and the evaluation design; the board approves the budget.
questions: Using Exhibits 1 to 3, list every explanation for the improvement at the program hospitals other than Bridge Home, and estimate which matter most.
Is a randomized stepped rollout ethical here? Under what conditions would it be unethical, and what would change your view?
What would you tell the board when it asks “does Bridge Home work?” Draft the two-sentence answer.
How should Grace handle the interpersonal dimension: Valdivia’s ownership, Feld’s credibility, the nurses’ frustration and her own preferences?
Design the minimum evaluation that would let the system know, in eighteen months, whether to continue funding the program.

perspectives.title: Expand now, measure better
perspectives.text: Given that staffing forces a sequential rollout anyway, expand to all three hospitals as fast as staffing allows, but in the order that capacity dictates, and invest in better measurement: medication adherence, navigator caseloads, and a matched comparison of similar patients. This position weighs the cost of delay to patients heavily and accepts weaker causal evidence. Its risk is that the system spends $1.6M a year for years without ever learning the true effect, and that the payer is unpersuaded by before-after data.

perspectives.title: Randomized stepped rollout
perspectives.text: Use a lottery to set the order of the three hospitals and a pre-registered analysis plan. Because the program cannot reach everyone at once, randomizing the order costs patients nothing relative to a non-random order and turns an unavoidable delay into a credible comparison. This position is strongest if Grace can show it does not slow the overall rollout. Its risks are that three hospitals is a small number of clusters, so the study may still be imprecise, and that it can be perceived as valuing data over patients.

perspectives.title: Redesign before scaling
perspectives.text: Feld’s analysis suggests the effect may be modest and context-dependent, and Lakeview and St. Brendan’s differ from the pilot sites in ways that matter to the mechanism (travel distance, language). Before spending $1.6M, adapt the program for those contexts, target patients without caregivers who are less likely to enroll, and test the adaptations. This position takes external validity seriously; its risk is delay and the appearance of indecision ahead of the payer penalty.

perspectives.title: The leadership reading
perspectives.text: The evidence question is genuinely uncertain, so the decision is also about process. Grace can make the evaluation a joint project, owned by Valdivia and Feld together, with pre-agreed criteria for success; frame randomization as a fair way to allocate a scarce resource; and commit publicly to what the system will do under each result. The risk is that a compromise that satisfies both leaders may still be the wrong design.

case.application: Player development faces the same disagreement constantly: a respected coach builds a program at the affiliates that struggled most, results improve, and an analyst points out regression to the mean, self-selection among players who embraced the program, and a concurrent change such as a new facility. The structure transfers directly. Because programs usually cannot reach every affiliate or player at once, a randomized rollout order is often available at no cost in coverage. The leadership challenge is the same as Grace’s: separating the evidence question from loyalty to the people involved, and designing the next season so that the organization knows more a year from now than it does today.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation of the result?

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: an airline identifies the 10 airports with the worst on-time departure records last summer and sends an operations improvement team to each. This summer, 8 of the 10 improve, by an average of 6 percentage points. Airports that were not visited improved by an average of 1 point. On-time performance at an airport has a year-to-year reliability of about 0.5.

options.text: The team caused a 6-point improvement.
The team caused a 5-point improvement (6 minus 1).
Much of the improvement is expected regression to the mean; the right comparison is with similarly bad airports that were not visited, which this analysis lacks.
The result is meaningless because 10 airports is too few.

questions.explanation: Airports were selected for being worst, so they carry unusually bad luck that will not repeat. With reliability around 0.5, a large share of their gap is expected to close without intervention. Comparing with the average non-visited airport does not remove this, because those airports were not selected on an extreme.

optionFeedback.a: A raw before-after change in selected extremes includes regression to the mean.
optionFeedback.b: Subtracting the change at average airports does not remove regression, because the comparison group was not selected on an extreme.
optionFeedback.d: Ten units can be informative with the right comparison; the problem is the comparison, not the count.

questions.prompt: A product analytics report says: “The new feature increased weekly sessions by 4% (95% CI −1% to 9%), p = .12.” Select every reasonable conclusion.

options.text: The data are compatible with no effect and with an effect of up to about 9%.
The feature has been shown not to work.
Whether to keep testing depends on the cost of the test and the value of a plausible effect.
There is an 88% chance the feature works.
The estimate is imprecise; a larger test would narrow the interval.

questions.explanation: The interval spans zero and meaningful positive values, so the study is inconclusive rather than negative. More data would narrow it, and whether it is worth collecting is an economic question. The p-value is not the probability the feature does not work.

questions.prompt: A company runs 200 A/B tests a year. Its best estimate is that 10% of tested ideas truly work. Tests have 50% power and use p < .05. Of the tests that come back significant, what percentage are expected to be true effects?
questions.working: True ideas: 20; significant true = 20 × 0.5 = 10. Null ideas: 180; significant false = 180 × 0.05 = 9. Share true = 10 / 19 ≈ 52.6%.
questions.explanation: Only about half of the “wins” are real, even though every test used a 5% threshold. With low priors and modest power, false positives make up a large share of significant results — Ioannidis’s argument applied to an organization.

questions.prompt: Identify the most serious flaw in the analyst’s argument.

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: “We tested our new call-center script on 30 agents per group. We tracked handle time, satisfaction, first-call resolution, transfers, escalations and upsell rate, in each of three regions. Upsell rate in the western region improved significantly (p = .03). The script works and should be rolled out nationally.”

options.text: The sample is too small for any conclusion.
With six outcomes in three regions (18 comparisons), one significant result is about what chance alone would produce; the finding needs a pre-specified confirmation.
Upsell rate is not a valid outcome for a call center.
The p-value should have been below .01.

questions.explanation: Eighteen comparisons at a 5% threshold produce roughly one false positive on average when nothing works. Reporting the one that succeeded is the undisclosed multiple testing that Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn showed can inflate false positives far above 5%. The finding is a hypothesis to test in a pre-specified study.

optionFeedback.a: Small samples are a concern (and inflate any real effect), but the decisive problem is the number of comparisons.
optionFeedback.c: Upsell can be a legitimate outcome; the issue is choosing it after the fact.
optionFeedback.d: A stricter threshold reduces but does not fix the problem of choosing among many comparisons.

questions.prompt: Which statement about this pattern is best supported?

stimulus.caption: Fictional summary of a literature on an employee-recognition program

options.text: Small studies are better because they can study the program more carefully.

The pattern is consistent with a significance filter and type-M error: small studies can be published only when their estimates are large, so the true effect is probably closer to the large preregistered studies.
The true effect is the average of the three rows, about 0.4.
Large studies dilute the effect by including people who did not engage with the program.

questions.explanation: Effects that shrink as studies grow, with the smallest effects in preregistered studies, are the signature of publication bias and exaggeration in low-powered studies. An unweighted average across rows inherits the bias.

optionFeedback.a: Smaller studies are noisier, not more careful; nothing in the data suggests better measurement.
optionFeedback.c: Averaging biased and unbiased estimates still yields a biased estimate.
optionFeedback.d: Possible in principle, but the preregistration and the size gradient point more strongly to filtering.

questions.prompt: Which design is this, and what is its key assumption?

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: a state awards extra tutoring funds to schools whose share of low-income students is at least 40%. An evaluator compares reading gains in schools at 38–39.9% with those at 40–41.9%.

options.text: Instrumental variables; the funding affects reading only through tutoring.
Regression discontinuity; schools just above and below 40% are otherwise similar and cannot precisely manipulate their reported share.
Difference-in-differences; parallel trends between funded and unfunded schools.
Randomized trial; funds were allocated by lottery.

questions.explanation: Treatment switches on at a threshold of a running variable, and units near the threshold are compared. The design fails if schools can shift their reported share to cross 40% or if something else also changes at 40%. The estimate applies to schools near the cutoff.

optionFeedback.a: The cutoff could be used as an instrument in a fuzzy design, but the comparison described is a discontinuity.
optionFeedback.c: No before-after comparison across groups is described.

questions.prompt: A health system wants to know whether a new discharge app reduces readmissions. It can afford to equip only half its 12 clinics this year and all of them next year. Clinic managers want to choose who goes first. What is the best next move?

options.text: Let managers choose; compare adopting with non-adopting clinics at year end, adjusting for size.
Assign the first six clinics by lottery, agree outcomes and analysis in advance, and compare the two groups before the second wave starts.
Equip all 12 clinics at once to avoid unfairness and compare this year with last year.
Wait for a published randomized trial of the app before adopting it.

questions.explanation: Capacity forces a phased rollout, so randomizing the order costs no coverage and removes selection: managers who volunteer may run better clinics. Pre-specification limits forking paths. This is the stepped-rollout logic from Lesson 3 and the case.

optionFeedback.a: Self-selected adopters differ in unmeasured ways; adjusting for size does not fix motivation or management quality.
optionFeedback.c: Not feasible within budget, and a before-after comparison confounds the app with everything else that changed.
optionFeedback.d: A published trial elsewhere may not transfer, and waiting forgoes a cheap way to learn locally.

questions.prompt: Rank these evaluations of a manager-training program from most to least credible as estimates of its causal effect on team turnover.

options.text: Managers who chose to attend vs. those who did not, adjusting for team size and tenure.
Training slots assigned by lottery among managers who applied; turnover compared a year later.
Turnover in the year after training vs. the year before, for trained managers only.
Change in turnover for trained managers vs. change for managers trained a year later, with similar trends before training.

questions.explanation: The lottery removes selection by design. The staggered comparison with checked pre-trends is a credible difference-in-differences. Adjusted self-selection leaves unmeasured motivation. A before-after comparison of trained managers alone has no counterfactual and is vulnerable to regression and secular trends.

questions.prompt: A professional services firm reports that consultants rated “exceptional” by clients have 30% higher utilization. Leadership proposes paying bonuses on client ratings. Select every legitimate concern.

options.text: Once ratings drive pay, consultants may lobby clients or avoid difficult engagements, so the ratings may stop measuring quality.
Client ratings may have low reliability, attenuating their relationship with real performance.
Utilization may cause high ratings rather than the reverse (busy consultants work with satisfied, repeat clients).
A 30% difference is too large to be real.
The relationship might not hold in other practice areas with different clients.

questions.explanation: Campbell’s and Goodhart’s principles predict that a rating used for pay will be gamed; unreliable ratings blur any true relationship; the direction of causation is unclear; and external validity across practices is not established. A large difference is not by itself implausible.

questions.prompt: What is the most important limitation for deciding whether to adopt the program in your organization?

stimulus.text: Fictional abstract: “In a randomized trial at one logistics company’s three warehouses (n = 1,240 workers who volunteered), a flexible-shift scheduling program reduced voluntary turnover from 18% to 12% over a year (95% CI for the difference: 2 to 10 points). Analyses were preregistered.” You run hospital nursing units.

options.text: The result is not statistically significant.
Randomization could not remove confounding.
External validity: volunteers in one logistics firm may differ from nurses in hospitals, and the mechanism (shift flexibility) may operate differently under clinical staffing constraints.
Preregistration makes the result less trustworthy.

questions.explanation: The study has strong internal validity: randomized, preregistered, with an interval excluding zero. The open question is transport: volunteers, one firm and a different kind of work. Whether shift flexibility is feasible and valued in nursing units is the mechanism question to examine.

optionFeedback.d: Preregistration constrains analytic flexibility and increases trust.

questions.prompt: A meta-analysis of 40 studies finds a pooled effect of d = 0.35 with a narrow confidence interval but very large heterogeneity. What is the best reading?

options.text: The program reliably produces an effect of about 0.35 everywhere.
The average is precisely estimated, but true effects vary a lot across settings; the key question is what moderates the effect and whether your setting resembles those where it worked.
High heterogeneity means the meta-analysis is invalid and should be ignored.
The narrow interval rules out publication bias.

questions.explanation: Large heterogeneity means the studies disagree more than chance predicts, so a single average conceals a wide range of true effects. Precision about the average is not precision about your case, and a narrow interval says nothing about publication bias.

optionFeedback.a: Heterogeneity contradicts a single common effect.
optionFeedback.d: Precision and bias are separate; a biased literature can produce a precise pooled estimate.

questions.prompt: A board member says: “We should only fund programs backed by randomized trials. Everything else is anecdote.” In 120–180 words, respond as an executive who respects evidence: where is the board member right, where is the position too rigid, and what decision rule would you propose instead?
questions.modelAnswer: The board member is right that randomized evidence is the best protection against confounding and selection, and that observational evidence has repeatedly misled — hormone therapy is the classic case. But a strict rule fails in three ways. Some effects are large and mechanistically obvious enough not to need a trial. Many of our decisions are one-off or local, so no trial exists, and a trial elsewhere may not transfer to our setting. And a meta-analysis of small published trials can itself be biased. I would propose a graded rule: weigh design quality, effect size, consistency across independent designs, mechanism and relevance to our population; require stronger evidence for expensive, irreversible commitments; and, where we can, build randomized or staggered rollouts into our own programs so that we generate the evidence we want to rely on.

rubric.criterion: Acknowledges the strength of randomization accurately
levels: 1 — mentions it without saying why it matters
2 — explains that randomization addresses confounding/selection, ideally with an example

rubric.criterion: Identifies limits of a strict RCT-only rule
levels: 2 — two limits (e.g. external validity, infeasible trials)
3 — three or more, including that top-ranked evidence can itself be biased
3 — graded weighing tied to stakes/reversibility and to generating evidence internally

reserve.prompt: A mutual-fund database includes only funds currently in operation. An analyst finds that the average fund in the database beat its benchmark over 15 years. What is the most important problem?

options.text: Regression to the mean.
Survivorship bias: funds that performed badly were more likely to close and disappear from the data.
Low statistical power.
Goodhart’s law.

reserve.explanation: Funds that closed or merged, usually after poor performance, are missing, so the surviving sample overstates average performance. Always ask what happened to the cases not in the data.

optionFeedback.a: Regression concerns re-measuring selected extremes, not missing cases.
optionFeedback.c: Power concerns detecting effects; the bias here arises from who is in the sample.
optionFeedback.d: No measure is being gamed here.

reserve.prompt: An outcome measure has reliability 0.36. A program’s true standardized effect is 0.5. What standardized effect would you expect to observe on average? Give a decimal.
reserve.explanation: Random measurement error attenuates observed effects by the square root of reliability. A study powered for 0.5 will often miss the effect it can actually see, about 0.3.

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: “Hospitals that adopted electronic checklists have 20% lower infection rates than those that did not. Therefore checklists reduce infections by 20%.”

options.text: Confounding: hospitals that adopt new safety tools may differ in resources, leadership and safety culture, all of which also reduce infections.
The effect is too large to be plausible.
Infection rates are not a valid outcome.
The comparison should use medians instead of means.

reserve.explanation: Adoption is chosen, so adopters likely differ in ways that also lower infections. The comparison mixes the checklist’s effect with those differences. A randomized or staggered rollout, or at least a difference-in-differences with pre-trends, is needed.

optionFeedback.b: Large effects can be real; the issue is the comparison.
optionFeedback.c: Infection rates are a reasonable outcome.
optionFeedback.d: The summary statistic is not the core problem.

reserve.prompt: Two years after a highly cited study of a negotiation technique, a large preregistered multi-site replication finds an effect about one-third the original size. Which explanation is most consistent with what you learned this week?

options.text: The replication team must have made errors.
The original was probably a low-powered study whose significant estimate was exaggerated; the replication is the better estimate of the average effect, though contexts may differ.
The technique stopped working because people learned about it.
Both estimates are equally credible, so the true effect is their average.

reserve.explanation: Shrinkage of this size is what type-M error and publication filtering predict. A large preregistered study is a better estimate, while still leaving room for genuine differences in context, as debates about replication fidelity remind us.

optionFeedback.a: Possible, but the default expectation from low-powered originals is shrinkage.
optionFeedback.c: Possible in principle, but no evidence is offered and the statistical explanation is sufficient.
optionFeedback.d: Estimates of unequal credibility should not be weighted equally.

assignment.title: Critique a Published Study

brief.text: Choose one of the four published studies below and write a structured critique of it, as you would for an executive team deciding whether to act on it. Each is a real study with a library record; read the full paper (or its freely available working-paper version where noted), not a press summary. Pick the study furthest from your own field if you want the hardest exercise, or the sports study if you want the most direct professional application.

items: [Bloom, Liang, Roberts & Ying (2015)](R-bloom-2015-does) — a randomized experiment on working from home at a call center (organizational behavior; field experiment).
[Yeager et al. (2019)](R-yeager-2019-national) — a preregistered national trial of a short growth-mindset intervention (education; randomized trial with heterogeneity analysis).
[Baicker et al. (2013)](R-baicker-2013-oregon) — the Oregon Medicaid lottery and clinical outcomes (healthcare policy; lottery-based randomized comparison with a power debate).
[Miller & Sanjurjo (2018)](R-miller-2018-surprised) — a measurement bias that reversed the classic “hot hand fallacy” result (sports performance; theory plus reanalysis).

brief.text: Use the template headings. Be specific: for every threat you raise, say which direction it would bias the result and roughly how much it could matter. End with your own evidence grade and a recommendation for a named, hypothetical decision-maker outside academia (for example a hospital system, a school district, a firm’s HR leadership or a sports organization).

Optional professional extension (not graded): add a short paragraph on what an equivalent study inside a player-development department would need — the comparison group, the outcome measure and its reliability, and the sample size — to be worth acting on.

Access note: library records mark which versions are believed to be freely available; the bibliographic details of these records were written without live verification in this build and are flagged for re-checking. If a link fails, search for the title and authors.

assignment.deliverable: A structured critique (1,000–1,500 words) of one listed study, ending with an evidence grade and a recommendation.

template.heading: Question
template.guidance: State the study’s research question and its main claim in one or two sentences. Is the claim causal or descriptive, and for which population?

template.heading: Design
template.guidance: Describe the comparison. What stands in for the counterfactual? What is the key assumption (random assignment, parallel trends, exclusion restriction, and so on), and is it defended?

template.heading: Measures
template.guidance: What are the outcomes and how were they measured? Comment on reliability, validity and whether the measure could be gamed or shaped by expectations.

template.heading: Sample
template.guidance: Who was studied, how were they recruited, who dropped out, and who never entered? Is the sample size adequate for a plausible effect?

template.heading: Analysis
template.guidance: Were outcomes and analyses pre-specified? How many comparisons were made? Report the main effect size in practical units with its interval.

template.heading: Threats to validity
template.guidance: List the most important threats (confounding, selection, attrition, measurement, multiple testing, publication bias). For each, give the likely direction and size of bias.

template.heading: Alternative explanations
template.guidance: What else could produce the findings? Which alternatives does the study rule out, and which remain?

template.heading: Generalizability
template.guidance: To which people, settings and times would you expect the result to transfer, and why? Argue from mechanism.

template.heading: What would change your mind
template.guidance: Name the specific evidence that would raise or lower your confidence, and give your overall evidence grade (strong / moderate / limited / very limited) with a one-paragraph recommendation for a named decision-maker.

rubric.criterion: Accurate description of question, design and measures

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Precise, correct account of claim, comparison, key assumption and outcomes, with page-level specificity.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Correct account with minor omissions.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Partly correct; key assumption or measure misdescribed.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Relies on summaries; significant errors.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Identifies the most important threats, states direction and plausible size of each, and distinguishes plausible from merely possible threats.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Identifies main threats with direction for most.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Generic list of threats without direction or prioritization.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Few or irrelevant threats; or dismisses the study without specifics.

rubric.criterion: Statistical interpretation (effect size, uncertainty, power, multiplicity)

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Interprets effect sizes in practical units with intervals; addresses power and multiple comparisons correctly.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Correct interpretation with minor gaps.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Relies on significance; limited attention to magnitude.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Misinterprets p-values or intervals.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Argues transport from mechanism, naming conditions under which the result would and would not hold.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Reasonable discussion of transfer with some mechanism.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Asserts the result does or does not generalize without argument.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Not addressed.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Proportionate evidence grade, clear recommendation tied to stakes, and specific evidence that would change the view.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Clear grade and recommendation; change-my-mind evidence somewhat general.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Recommendation not clearly linked to the analysis.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No grade or recommendation.

prompts: Recall a decision in your career that was justified by a before-after comparison after a bad stretch. With what you now know about regression to the mean, how confident are you that the intervention caused the improvement?
Which metric in your current work is most at risk of becoming a target that stops measuring what it was meant to? What would you watch for?
When you disagreed with a colleague about what the evidence showed, how much of the disagreement was about the evidence and how much about the people or the stakes? What would have changed your mind?
Identify one recurring program or practice in your work that could be rolled out in a randomized or staggered order at no cost in coverage. What would you learn?

review.front: Why do the worst performers on a noisy metric usually improve without help?
review.back: They were selected partly for bad luck, which is redrawn on re-measurement; the stable part persists, so the group drifts toward the mean (regression to the mean).

If the null model (usually no effect) and its assumptions were true, data at least this extreme would arise about 3% of the time. It is not the probability the claim is true or a measure of importance.

review.front: What two features of a confidence interval matter most?
review.back: Its location (the plausible magnitudes) and its width (how much the study actually taught you).

review.front: Three inputs determine how likely a significant result is to be true. Which?
review.back: The prior probability the idea is true, the study’s power, and the significance threshold (plus any bias).

review.front: What is a type M error, and when is it worst?
review.back: An exaggerated estimate of magnitude among significant results; worst when power is low.

review.front: Name four researcher degrees of freedom.
review.back: Choosing among outcomes; adding data after peeking; adding or dropping covariates; dropping conditions or subgroups (also outlier rules and time windows).

review.front: What did the 100-study replication project find, in brief?
review.back: About 97% of originals were significant vs. about 36% of replications, and replication effects were about half the original size.

review.front: What is the key assumption of difference-in-differences?
review.back: Parallel trends: without treatment, the treated and comparison groups would have changed by the same amount.

review.front: Why did the randomized hormone-therapy trial contradict observational studies?
review.back: Women who chose therapy were plausibly healthier in other ways (confounding); randomization removed that difference.

review.front: Give the collider structure behind “among promoted employees, two good traits look negatively related”.
review.back: Promotion depends on both traits; selecting on promotion induces a negative correlation even if the traits are unrelated.

review.front: Why is “we compared participants with non-participants” weak?
review.back: Because the naive difference equals the true effect plus selection bias — how the groups would have differed anyway.

review.front: What does low reliability do to an observed effect?
review.back: Attenuates it toward zero, roughly by the square root of reliability, causing false negatives.

review.front: Significance vs. importance: which does a huge sample guarantee?
review.back: Significance (detectability) of even trivial effects; importance requires a practical magnitude judged against costs.
The more a quantitative indicator is used for social decisions, the more it is corrupted and the more it distorts the process it monitors.

review.front: Why can a meta-analysis be precise and wrong?
review.back: Pooling reduces random error but not bias shared by the included studies, such as publication bias.

review.front: What does an evidence hierarchy rank?
review.back: Designs by their typical protection against bias — not truth. Adjust for size, consistency, mechanism and relevance.

preview.text: The habits from this week recur throughout the semester. Week 5 asks which leadership theories have evidence behind them. Week 8 returns to Goodhart’s law when you design metrics and incentives for a department. Week 10 turns uncertainty into scenario analysis and expected value. Week 12 treats staggered rollouts and dashboards as implementation tools, and Week 13 asks how to decide responsibly when the evidence is incomplete.
